# rival

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.rival.0)
[dca5e9634b898353] (h005.fork5.p.rival.0)
Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: body

BODY
The material gives four facts: recurring arguments over ordinary chores; agreements whose meaning gets disputed later; shifting work schedules; and one friend now avoiding the conversation. Worth noticing first: these are four different kinds of problem, and treating all four as one argument about chores is probably part of why the arguments recur.

1. The "what did we agree" disputes point at the form of the agreements, not just their content. Verbal, in-passing agreements about chores are almost designed for retrospective divergence: "I'll sort the kitchen" can mean surfaces, or surfaces plus floor, or "when I get to it." When memories diverge, the resulting argument feels like bad faith but is mostly underspecification. The remedy is not more sincerity but more form: one shared, visible record of task, person, day, and what counts as done, plus a pre-agreed rule for disputed items (e.g., disputed tasks rotate by default) so divergence doesn't require an adjudication every time. Caveat: a written system can read as bureaucratic or accusatory among friends, and if it arrives while one person is already withdrawing it can be received as a weapon. Keep it minimal — one shared list — frame it as protecting the friendship, and introduce it in a calm jointly-agreed moment, never mid-dispute.

2. Changing schedules mean any fixed rota will keep breaking, and each break re-opens allocation — exactly the conversation that is failing. I'd conjecture that what's needed is not a stricter rota but a cheap, scheduled renegotiation step: a short weekly reset (ten minutes, or even a group message) where the coming week's schedules determine who takes what. Then schedule change stops being a breach and becomes the normal input.

3. The avoidance is the element I'd treat as most serious. A chore arrangement accepted by two of three has no legitimacy; it will be quietly ignored and breed resentment. Avoidance here usually means the conversation has become costly for that person — it may feel like being ganged up on, or like a lecture, or their schedule may make them look bad. Escalating pressure in the same format tends to deepen avoidance. Cheaper moves: talk one-on-one rather than two-against-one; allow asynchronous channels; offer limited choices ("Tuesday or Sunday for the bins?") instead of open debate; and ask directly, once and gently, what makes these talks hard for them. If they still avoid low-cost channels, that has stopped being a chore problem and become a friendship-level problem worth naming as such.

4. What I can't see: only one side is given. It's possible the asker's tone reads to the others as policing; possible the real grievance is uneven effort and chore-talk is merely where it surfaces; possible there is unrelated strain. So the first move may be a meta-conversation — not "here's the new system" but "we keep ending up in the same argument; none of us likes it; can we agree it's broken and try something small?" Agreement that the loop is broken is cheaper to obtain than agreement on any particular rota.

Conjectured sequence: repair the participation channel first, then the meta-agreement, then a minimal written list with a dispute rule, then the weekly schedule-keyed reset. Two things stay genuinely open. First, the fairness metric — equal tasks, equal time, or weighted by time and unpleasantness — and shifting schedules may make equal-time unfair; it has to be chosen explicitly rather than assumed shared. Second, if some reinterpretation of past agreements is strategic (escaping a task one regrets accepting), explicitness still helps by raising the cost of reinterpretation — but it will surface an underlying fairness grievance rather than dissolve it, and that grievance will need discussion, not documentation.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
